output:
To: localrate.example/biz/harbourline-van-works
Replying to: none
Cc: none
Subject: Draft review — 3 stars

Harbourline fitted out my 2021 Ford Transit for my mobile dog-grooming business, and I’ll start with the good part: the stainless tub and ramp are genuinely excellent. Dogs walk right in like celebrities arriving at a spa, and the tub-and-ramp setup is still my favourite thing about the van. Five stars for that part.

Unfortunately, on October 27, a fitting on the hot-water line let go halfway through a groom. Suddenly there was water across the floor and down into the cabinet, plus a 110-pound Bernese in the tub who thought this was all extremely entertaining.

That was Moose. To be clear, Moose was fine. Moose was better than fine. He sat there through the whole flood like a king whose indoor pool had finally been installed, completely unbothered while I was the one screaming. He eventually went home towel-dried and only half-groomed, still living his best life. I was less relaxed.

The van was off the road from October 27 until November 6. I lost six bookings, on top of having to cancel the rest of that first day. When your business is the van, that’s a serious disruption, not just an annoying afternoon with a lot of towels.

Stuff breaks, though. I understand that, and the leak itself isn’t what made me angry. What got under my skin was the initial response: I was told these lines don’t usually just let go, that it could be from running the heater dry or hanging things off the pipe, and that if it was “user error” it wouldn’t be covered. There would also be a $180 diagnostic fee, with the earliest appointment nearly a week away.

I’ve never run the heater dry, and nobody hangs anything off that pipe—it’s behind a cabinet door. Having possible explanations floated before anyone had inspected the van was frustrating, but having the conversation start with why I might be responsible, while I was cancelling work, felt worse.

Credit where it’s due: once Glenn looked at it, he found that the compression fitting on the outlet was a cheaper one his supplier had substituted. He said that was on Harbourline, replaced all the corresponding fittings on the hot side, and knocked off the $180 as goodwill. He owned the problem and put it right, and that deserves to be part of the review too.

So why three stars? The finished tub and ramp are great, and the eventual resolution was fair. But the lost bookings, the time off the road, and the initial assumption about user error took the shine off the whole experience. The final email was the response I wish I’d received at the beginning.

For other groomers or trades considering a fitout: get the warranty details in writing. The invoice did include a 12-month workmanship warranty, but I’d also ask specifically how “misuse or user error” is determined, what diagnostic charges apply, and what happens to those charges if the problem turns out to be a part or installation issue.

No personal beef with Glenn—just an honest account of a good fitout feature, a ridiculous flood, one delighted dog, and a repair process that started badly but ended with Harbourline taking responsibility.
